hook.line: Thirty-three points on a cross. One fox and thirteen geese: one hunts, the others surround.
hook.say: Quack! Let me show you the story of Fox and Geese.

ch.t: A hunt game of northern Europe
ch.say: People have played it for hundreds of years.
p: A hunt game: one fox against a flock of geese. Its old form is taken to be the halatafl of the Icelandic Grettis saga, and it was played by the 14th century at the latest.
Edward IV of England (reigned 1461–83) had sets made with “two foxis and 26 hounds of silver overgilt”. It has relatives all over Europe.

ch.say: The fox and the geese have completely different jobs!
ch.cap: The cross of 33 points: the fox in the middle, the 13 geese on the near side
p: The fox moves one step along a line, or jumps over a goose next to it and takes it. It may jump again and again, and capturing is never compulsory.
The geese only step, and they cannot capture. But if they crowd the fox until it cannot move, they win. With five geese or fewer left, the fox wins.
tip: With correct play the geese are said to always win under the original rules, so many players play twice with the roles swapped and compare captures or how fast the fox is trapped.

ch.say: The number of geese changes the game.
